description:
The A. G. Leventis Gallery opened in central Nicosia in 2014 to share the art collections associated with Anastasios G. Leventis and his foundation.

Its Paris, Greek and Cyprus collections connect European painting with the development of modern Greek and Cypriot art. A separate collection of gold coins and medals adds another perspective on the histories represented in the gallery.

The Albertina in Vienna is especially associated with art on paper. Its collection of drawings and prints traces its origins to Duke Albert of Saxe-Teschen in the eighteenth century.

Works ranging from the late Gothic period to the present connect the study of drawing with the history of printmaking. The collection offers a view of artistic invention through both finished images and the marks of an artist’s working process.

The Alte Pinakothek is part of the Bavarian State Painting Collections in Munich’s Kunstareal. Opened in 1836, it grew from collections formed by the rulers of the Wittelsbach dynasty.

Its principal focus is European painting from the fourteenth to the eighteenth century. German Renaissance, Italian, Dutch and Flemish works give the collection its breadth, with Dürer and Rubens among its central figures.

The Neue Pinakothek in Munich is the Bavarian State Painting Collections’ museum of nineteenth-century art. Its origins lie in King Ludwig I’s collection of the contemporary painting of his time.

The collection follows European art from the late eighteenth century towards modernism, including Romanticism, Realism and Impressionism. The museum building is undergoing renovation; the official website gives the current arrangements for visiting selections from the collection.

MuMa, the Musée d’art moderne André Malraux, is Le Havre’s museum of fine art. Its collection is particularly strong in painting from the second half of the nineteenth century and the early twentieth century.

Works associated with Eugène Boudin, Impressionism and the development of modern painting connect the collection with Normandy’s coast and artistic life. Municipal acquisitions and private gifts, including the Senn collection, helped shape its character.

The Belvedere is a museum institution in Vienna with collections extending from medieval art to the present. Its historic palaces and Belvedere 21 provide distinct settings for Austrian art and its international connections.

Important areas include Austrian Baroque painting, Biedermeier and Viennese modernism. Gustav Klimt’s paintings are a particular strength, alongside works by artists such as Egon Schiele and Ferdinand Georg Waldmüller.

The Picture Gallery of Vienna’s Kunsthistorisches Museum developed from the collections of the Habsburg dynasty. It is one part of a wider museum whose collections also include antiquities and decorative arts.

The gallery is especially strong in Venetian Renaissance and Flemish Baroque painting, alongside early Netherlandish and German Renaissance art. Its works by Pieter Bruegel the Elder are a defining feature of the collection.

The Leopold Museum in Vienna grew from the collection assembled by Rudolf Leopold. It brings together a substantial body of Austrian art, with a particular emphasis on the artistic changes around 1900.

Egon Schiele’s paintings and works on paper form a major focus. The collection also provides a setting for understanding Viennese modernism through artists including Gustav Klimt and Oskar Kokoschka.

The Groeningemuseum is part of Musea Brugge in Bruges. Its collection follows six centuries of art connected with the Low Countries and Belgium.

Early Netherlandish painting is a central strength, including works by Jan van Eyck, Hans Memling and Gerard David. Later holdings extend through Bruges Neoclassicism, Symbolism and Flemish Expressionism to modern and postwar art.

The Museum of Fine Arts Ghent, known as MSK, preserves a collection whose history reaches back to the formation of a public art collection around the turn of the nineteenth century.

Its holdings span European art from the Middle Ages to the present, bringing painting and sculpture together with works on paper and other media. The collection connects the artistic history of the southern Netherlands with later Belgian and international developments.

The Royal Museum of Fine Arts Antwerp, or KMSKA, holds a collection extending from early Netherlandish painting to modern art. Its history is closely connected with Antwerp’s artistic institutions and collectors.

Flemish painting, including Rubens and the Antwerp Baroque, is a particular strength. Extensive groups of works by James Ensor and Rik Wouters connect those older traditions with the experiments of modern Belgian art.

The Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium form a group of museums in Brussels. Their collections range from the fifteenth century to contemporary art, with a strong focus on Belgium and the former Southern Netherlands.

Paintings, sculptures, drawings and prints provide the core of the holdings. The Old Masters, Magritte, Wiertz and Meunier museums offer different ways into the collection’s history and its individual artists.

The National Gallery of Canada is based in Ottawa and was established in 1880. Its collection and research programmes explore Canadian art in relation to wider artistic histories.

Historical and contemporary Canadian art, Indigenous art and European art are important areas of the collection. These holdings connect different traditions, communities and periods rather than presenting Canadian art as a single uniform story.

The Centre of Visual Arts and Research, or CVAR, opened in 2014 on Ermou Street inside Nicosia’s old city walls. It houses the collections assembled by Costas and Rita Severis.

Paintings made by travellers to Cyprus sit alongside photographs, costumes, books and memorabilia. Together they document changing views of the island, its people and its relationships with neighbouring regions.

Skagens Museum is devoted to the artists who made the fishing town of Skagen an important meeting place in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

Paintings, drawings and related material connect the artists’ work with the local community and their shared social life. The museum’s wider organisation also includes the former homes of the Anchers and Holger Drachmann.

Statens Museum for Kunst, known as SMK, is Denmark’s national gallery in Copenhagen. Its collection spans roughly seven centuries of European, Danish and international art.

Danish and Nordic painting, including the Danish Golden Age, is a major focus. Older European art, French modernism and later international work place that history in a broader context, alongside the museum’s extensive holdings of works on paper.

The Ateneum in Helsinki is part of the Finnish National Gallery. Its collection traces the development of Finnish art from eighteenth-century portraiture to the experiments of the twentieth century and later work.

Paintings and sculptures are complemented by drawings, watercolours, sketches and artists’ notebooks. These works connect the familiar images of Finland’s artistic Golden Age with changing international influences and individual working methods.

The Musée Condé occupies the Château de Chantilly. Its collections were assembled by Henri d’Orléans, Duke of Aumale, and given with the estate to the Institut de France.

The picture galleries preserve the character of a nineteenth-century collector’s museum. Italian and French painting are important strengths, complemented by drawings, manuscripts, sculpture and decorative arts associated with the château.

The Musée Marmottan Monet occupies a former private residence in Paris. Its collections combine the legacy of Paul Marmottan with major gifts from artists’ families and other collectors.

Claude Monet and Berthe Morisot are central to its identity, alongside other Impressionist and later artists. Earlier paintings, illuminated manuscripts, sculpture and the house’s Empire-style decoration give the museum a broader historical setting.

The Musée de l’Orangerie in Paris brings together two distinctive groups of paintings: Claude Monet’s large Water Lilies decorations and the collection associated with Jean Walter and Paul Guillaume.

The Water Lilies form an immersive ensemble conceived around Monet’s late work. Paintings by artists including Cézanne, Renoir, Matisse, Picasso, Modigliani and Soutine offer a different, more intimate view of the development of modern art.

The Musée des Beaux-Arts de Rouen grew from a public collection formed during the French Revolutionary period and the museum established by the Chaptal decree of 1801.

Its paintings, sculptures, drawings and decorative arts range from the fifteenth century to recent work. Seventeenth-century painting and nineteenth-century art are major strengths, with the Depeaux donation helping establish its important Impressionist collection.

The Musée d’Orsay occupies a former railway station beside the Seine in Paris. Its collections concentrate on the artistic changes of the period from 1848 to 1914.

Painting and sculpture are joined by photography, drawings, decorative arts and architectural material. Realism, Impressionism, Post-Impressionism and other movements are considered within the wider visual culture of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

The Musée d’arts de Nantes brings together Western art from the Middle Ages to the present. Its buildings combine historic museum spaces with modern additions.

Old Master and nineteenth-century works sit within a collection that also has a substantial modern and contemporary component. Paintings, sculpture, photographs, video and installations make it possible to follow changes across several centuries and different forms of art.

The Musée national Picasso-Paris preserves a wide-ranging collection of Pablo Picasso’s work and personal archives. Major parts entered the French national collections through arrangements with the artist’s heirs.

Paintings and sculptures are complemented by drawings, notebooks, prints, photographs and documents. The relationship between finished works and preparatory material makes the collection especially useful for following Picasso’s changing ideas and creative processes.

The Palais des Beaux-Arts is Lille’s major fine arts museum, located on Place de la République. Its collections bring together painting, sculpture, decorative arts and archaeological material.

Flemish art is an important strength, alongside Italian Renaissance works, Spanish painting and French art of the nineteenth century. These different schools give the museum a broad European scope rather than a focus on a single artist or movement.

The Staatliche Kunstsammlungen Dresden are a network of museums centred on Dresden, with further museums in Leipzig and Herrnhut. Their collections encompass art and cultural objects from many parts of the world.

The Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister in the Zwinger’s Semper Building is one part of this wider institution. Other collections include modern art at the Albertinum, prints and drawings, porcelain, decorative arts and the historic treasures of the Grünes Gewölbe.

The Germanisches Nationalmuseum in Nuremberg studies the art, history and material culture of German-speaking regions. Its scope extends from archaeology to the present.

Paintings and sculpture form part of a much broader collection that includes musical instruments, textiles, furniture, prints, manuscripts and everyday objects. This combination places works of art alongside the social and cultural settings in which they were made and used.

The Hamburger Kunsthalle preserves a public art collection in Hamburg spanning the Middle Ages to the present. Its scope allows European art to be considered across many periods.

Old Masters, nineteenth-century painting, modernism and contemporary art form the main areas. Sculpture, works on paper and media art broaden the collection beyond painting and connect older traditions with more recent artistic practices.

The Staatliche Kunsthalle Karlsruhe holds a collection of European art shaped in part by the collecting of Baden’s margraves. Paintings are complemented by extensive holdings of drawings and prints.

The collection spans medieval and Renaissance art, Dutch and French painting, nineteenth-century movements and modern work. Its main building is undergoing renovation; the official visitor information identifies the other Karlsruhe venues used for exhibitions during this period.

The Städel Museum in Frankfurt am Main was established in 1815 through the bequest of banker and collector Johann Friedrich Städel. It continues the tradition of a civic museum foundation.

Its collections span art from the early fourteenth century to the present, including paintings, sculpture, photography, drawings and prints. Old Masters, modernism and contemporary art provide connected views of more than seven centuries of artistic change.

The Athens museum of the Basil and Elise Goulandris Foundation makes accessible the collection assembled by its founders over several decades. It is based on Eratosthenous Street in the city.

The collection brings modern and contemporary Greek art into conversation with international artists. Works by figures such as Cézanne, van Gogh, Picasso and Giacometti sit within a broader account of the founders’ individual tastes and collecting interests.

The National Gallery – Alexandros Soutsos Museum in Athens is devoted especially to the history of modern Greek art. Founded in 1900, it later incorporated the Alexandros Soutsos estate.

Its collections follow Greek painting and other arts from post-Byzantine traditions to the present. Sculpture, prints and works in newer media broaden that history, while a collection of Western European painting offers additional points of comparison.

The Galleria Borghese in Rome preserves a collection whose core was assembled by Cardinal Scipione Borghese in the early seventeenth century.

Ancient sculpture and mosaics share the collection with paintings and sculpture from the fifteenth to nineteenth centuries. Works by Caravaggio, Raphael and Titian, together with sculptures by Bernini and Canova, are central to the museum’s identity.

The Gallerie dell’Accademia in Venice occupy the historic Santa Maria della Carità complex, incorporating a church, convent and former confraternity building.

The collection follows the development of Venetian and Veneto painting, particularly from the fourteenth to the eighteenth century. Giovanni Bellini, Giorgione, Titian, Tintoretto, Veronese and Tiepolo are among the artists through whom that history can be explored.

The Centraal Museum in Utrecht brings together art, design, fashion and the history of the city. Its collections connect local stories with wider artistic developments.

Painting and historical objects are complemented by modern design and contemporary work. Material associated with Gerrit Rietveld, Dick Bruna and other Utrecht makers provides distinctive points of entry into the collection and its research archives.

The Kröller-Müller Museum in Otterlo grew from the collection assembled by Helene and Anton Kröller-Müller. Vincent van Gogh’s work holds a particularly important place in its history.

Paintings and drawings by Van Gogh form part of a broader collection of modern art. The museum’s sculpture garden extends the encounter with art into its wooded surroundings, connecting the indoor collection with the landscape.

The Mauritshuis in The Hague houses the Royal Picture Gallery, a collection rooted in the eighteenth-century collecting of Prince William V and later expanded through purchases and gifts.

Dutch and Flemish painting of the seventeenth century is its central strength. Works by Rembrandt, Vermeer, Frans Hals and other artists offer close views of portraiture, landscape, still life and scenes of everyday life.

Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen is an art museum in Rotterdam with collections reaching from the Middle Ages to contemporary work. Its holdings developed through the gifts and interests of successive collectors.

Paintings, sculpture, drawings and prints are joined by design, photography, video and installations. Early Netherlandish and Dutch painting, modern movements and Surrealism provide different routes through this broad collection; the Depot offers a separate setting for its care and storage.

The Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam preserves art and objects that illuminate the history of the Netherlands and its connections with the wider world.

Dutch painting and sculpture from the late Middle Ages onward are major strengths, with seventeenth-century painting at the core. European and Asian art, works on paper and decorative objects broaden the collection beyond the history of painting alone.

The Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam is dedicated to the life and work of Vincent van Gogh. Its collection grew from works preserved by the artist’s family.

Paintings, drawings, letters and archival material allow his changing ideas and working methods to be followed closely. Art by his contemporaries, artists who influenced him and later admirers places his achievement within the wider art of the nineteenth century and its aftermath.

Auckland Art Gallery Toi o Tāmaki opened in 1888 with founding gifts of European and British art. It has developed alongside the city of Auckland and the cultural life of Aotearoa New Zealand.

Its collections encompass historical, modern and contemporary New Zealand art, with important Māori and Pacific work. International paintings, sculpture and prints connect these holdings with artistic traditions across Asia, Europe and the Americas.

The National Museum in Oslo brings together Norway’s national collections of art, architecture and design. Its remit includes preserving, researching and sharing these collections with the public.

The museum connects older and contemporary art with decorative arts and design rather than treating them as separate histories. Its wider organisation also includes dedicated architecture displays and Villa Stenersen.

The National Museum in Kraków is a museum organisation with collections and galleries distributed across several sites in the city. Its holdings connect Polish art with wider European and cultural histories.

The Main Building is associated with decorative art and twentieth- and twenty-first-century Polish art, while other branches preserve different parts of the collection. Paintings, sculpture, works on paper and historic objects give the institution a scope broader than any single building.

The National Museum in Warsaw preserves art from Poland and many other regions, ranging from antiquity to the present. It is a broad art museum rather than a collection devoted to one period.

Paintings and sculpture are complemented by drawings, prints, photographs, coins, decorative arts and design. Together these holdings offer ways to compare Polish artistic traditions with international histories and different kinds of cultural objects.

The Museo Nacional Thyssen-Bornemisza in Madrid grew from a collection assembled over two generations of the Thyssen-Bornemisza family. Its principal collection was acquired by the Spanish state in 1993.

The paintings span seven centuries of Western art, from early Italian and Netherlandish works to twentieth-century movements. Impressionism, German Expressionism and American painting give the collection distinctive strengths alongside its Old Masters.

Nationalmuseum in Stockholm brings together painting, sculpture, works on paper, applied arts and design. Swedish art is considered alongside wider European traditions.

Its collections are particularly strong in Swedish eighteenth- and nineteenth-century painting, Dutch seventeenth-century art and French eighteenth-century works. Decorative arts and design extend from the late Middle Ages into the present, broadening the museum’s account of visual culture.

The Kunsthaus Zürich holds an art collection spanning the Middle Ages to contemporary practice. Its range includes painting, sculpture, works on paper, photography, installations and digital media.

Swiss art, Impressionism and modernism are significant areas, alongside major groups associated with Alberto Giacometti, Edvard Munch and Zurich Dada. Contemporary work and changing presentations place these histories in dialogue with the present.

The Kunstmuseum Basel preserves the city’s public art collection. Its historic core was the Amerbach Cabinet, acquired by Basel in 1661 and subsequently made accessible to the public.

The collection reaches from the late Middle Ages to the present. Paintings associated with Konrad Witz and the Holbein family form important early strengths, alongside later European art, modernism and contemporary work.

Museum Rietberg is set in Zurich’s Rieterpark, where historic villas are joined by a modern extension with substantial underground spaces.

The collection focuses on art and cultural objects from Asia, Africa, the Americas and Oceania, with Swiss masks also represented. Its combination of collections, exhibitions and architecture provides a setting for exploring artistic traditions across different regions of the world.

The National Gallery in London was founded in 1824 and moved to its Trafalgar Square building in 1838. It preserves the nation’s collection of paintings in the Western European tradition.

The collection follows painting from the late thirteenth to the early twentieth century. Italian Renaissance, Dutch and Flemish painting, and later French and British art allow artists and subjects to be compared across several centuries.

National Museum Cardiff combines art with natural history in the city’s civic centre. Its art collections explore Welsh culture in relation to European and international traditions.

Paintings, drawings, sculpture, ceramics and silver span roughly five centuries. French Impressionist and Post-Impressionist art is a particular strength, alongside historic and contemporary works connected with Wales.

The Scottish National Gallery, also known as the National, is located on the Mound in central Edinburgh. It forms part of the National Galleries of Scotland.

Its collection brings Scottish and international art together, from early European painting to works of the twentieth century. Scottish painting of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries is a major focus alongside artists such as Titian, Rembrandt, Velázquez and the Impressionists.

Tate is a museum organisation with galleries in London, Liverpool and St Ives. Tate Britain and Tate Modern are its two London museums, each with a distinct focus.

The collection encompasses British art from the sixteenth century onward and international modern and contemporary art. Works are shared through the different galleries, exhibitions, research and digital resources, so the institution’s collection extends beyond a single building or city.

The Courtauld Gallery occupies Somerset House in central London and is closely connected with the Courtauld Institute’s teaching and research in art history and conservation.

Its paintings, drawings, prints, sculpture and decorative arts reach from the Middle Ages to more recent work. Impressionist and Post-Impressionist painting is a defining strength, including works collected by Samuel Courtauld from artists such as Manet, Cézanne and van Gogh.

The Art Institute of Chicago is an art museum in Grant Park, Chicago. Its broad collections connect artistic traditions from around the world and many different periods.

Impressionist and Post-Impressionist painting is a particular strength, alongside American art and extensive holdings of prints, drawings, textiles and decorative arts. The collection’s range makes it possible to compare familiar paintings with works in other media and cultural settings.

The Cleveland Museum of Art opened in 1916 in Cleveland’s University Circle area. It was founded as a public resource supported by local donors and endowments.

Its collection spans several thousand years and artistic traditions from around the world. Paintings, sculpture and works on paper sit alongside textiles, decorative objects and newer media, with Asian art an important part of the museum’s collecting history.

The Detroit Institute of Arts was founded in 1885 and moved to its Woodward Avenue building in 1927. It is a broad art museum serving Detroit and the surrounding region.

American and European art form part of collections that also include African, Asian, Indigenous American, Oceanic, Islamic and ancient art. Diego Rivera’s Detroit Industry fresco cycle is a defining work associated with the museum and the city’s industrial history.

The J. Paul Getty Museum operates at two sites in the Los Angeles area: the Getty Center in Brentwood and the Getty Villa in Pacific Palisades.

The Center is associated with European art, modern architecture and views across Los Angeles. The Villa focuses on ancient Greek and Roman art in a building inspired by an ancient Roman house; the two sites represent different parts of the museum’s collections.

The Minneapolis Institute of Art, often called Mia, preserves a collection drawn from cultures across six continents. Its scope reaches across roughly five thousand years of artistic production.

Asian, European, African and American art are joined by global contemporary work. The collection connects paintings and sculpture with textiles, decorative objects and other forms of making, encouraging comparisons across different places and periods.

The Smithsonian’s National Museum of Asian Art occupies the connected Freer Gallery of Art and Arthur M. Sackler Gallery on the National Mall in Washington, DC.

Its collections encompass art from China, Japan, Korea, South and Southeast Asia, the ancient Near East and the Islamic world. The Freer Gallery also preserves a significant group of American works, chiefly from the late nineteenth century.

The Philadelphia Museum of Art occupies a campus along the Benjamin Franklin Parkway. Its collections and institutional history grew from the city’s artistic life and the Centennial Exhibition of 1876.

The collection ranges across thousands of years and many cultures, encompassing painting, sculpture, decorative arts, textiles, prints and photography. Modern art, including major Dada and Surrealist works, forms one distinctive part of this wider history.

The Smithsonian American Art Museum explores American visual culture from the colonial period to the present. Its main museum is in central Washington, DC.

Painting, sculpture, photography, craft and newer media contribute to this account. The collections include American Impressionism, New Deal art and work by self-taught, African American and Latino artists.

The Yale Center for British Art in New Haven opened in 1977 through the gift of Paul Mellon. Its purpose-built home on the Yale campus was designed by Louis I. Kahn.

The collection follows British art across more than five centuries through paintings, sculpture, drawings, prints, rare books and archives. Portraiture, landscape and sporting art are particular strengths, with later work extending the study of British art and its global connections.
